UnaFinancial Enters South Africa With a Digital Lending Service
summary:
Kredio offers South African consumers digital loans ranging from R500 to R8,000, with repayment terms of 7 to 45 days. The application process is easy: an automated credit check delivers a decision, and approved funds are paid to the borrower's bank account within minutes, with no branch visits. The company is registered with the National Credit Regulator.
South Africa has one of the most developed financial markets on the continent, and demand for credit outside traditional banks is growing. Alternative lenders increased personal loan originations by 11.5% year-on-year in Q1 2025, and 35% of surveyed consumers plan to use alternative credit within the next year. Yet formal credit remains out of reach for many account holders. According to the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025, 81% of adults had a financial account, but only 13% borrowed from a formal financial institution.
Sergey Sedov, CEO of UnaFinancial, commented: "Expanding access to credit at scale depends on the ability to assess borrowers quickly and accurately. Over the years, we have built lending technology and scoring models that do this in markets with very different environments. For South Africa, we have adapted this infrastructure to local regulation, data sources and borrowing behaviour. We believe the service will meet the needs of South African borrowers and help close the gap in access to finance."

Two in Five Financial Services Leaders Say AI Capability Gaps Have Cost Them Business
summary:
​​​Two in five (40%) financial services directors and C-Suite professionals say their organisation has lost a competitive bid or client opportunity partly because of AI capability concerns, according to new research from Kaplan UK - a leading provider of professional education, apprenticeship training, and enterprise upskilling.
The findings suggest that capability gaps are beginning to have a direct commercial impact in a sector where AI adoption is already a significant strategic priority.
More than four in five (81%) C-Suite respondents in financial services told Kaplan that AI adoption and expansion is a high or top organisational priority over the next 12 months, compared with 74% of leaders across industries overall.
Financial services C-Suite teams were also more likely to say they are confident their organisation has a clearly defined AI strategy that is understood at senior level.
However, Kaplan’s research suggests investment in the sector remains more heavily weighted towards technology than the workforce expected to use it.
Half (50%) of financial services C-Suite respondents said their organisation has placed greater emphasis on investing in AI tools and technology, compared with just 17% who said greater emphasis has been placed on workforce capability development.
The findings are published in Kaplan’s new whitepaper, From AI to ROI: Who owns the problem? which examines the relationship between AI investment, workforce capability and business performance. The Kaplan study is grounded in the views of 1,000 UK employees, 600 HR and L&D professionals, and 600 company directors and C-Suite leaders.
Financial services leaders also estimated that fewer than half of the employees (45%) expected to work with AI are genuinely proficient, compared to 79% of employees in the sector that are confident in using AI productively.
Taken together, the findings point to a potential gap between strategic ambition and organisations’ ability to translate AI investment into day-to-day capability. Despite high levels of leadership focus on AI, many financial services businesses are investing more heavily in the technology itself than in developing the people expected to apply it.
​​​Chiraag Swaly, Head of Data and Technology Curriculum at Kaplan, said: “Financial services organisations clearly recognise the strategic importance of AI. The sector is prioritising adoption and leaders are putting AI strategies in place, but the research suggests that technology investment alone is not enough to generate a return.
“When four in ten C-Suite leaders say AI capability concerns have contributed to losing a bid or client opportunity, workforce capability becomes a commercial issue rather than simply a training issue.
“Financial services employees operate in environments where judgement, accuracy and the appropriate use of technology matter enormously. Giving people access to AI is therefore only one part of the challenge. Organisations also need to ensure employees can apply those tools effectively in the context of their roles.
“The gap between investment in technology and investment in workforce capability is significant. Closing it will require organisations to treat the skills needed to use AI as part of the transformation itself, rather than something that follows deployment.”
The findings reflect a broader pattern identified by Kaplan across UK businesses. While organisations are investing heavily in AI, the research suggests workforce development is not always progressing at the same pace.
Across industries, 54% of C-Suite and director respondents said AI-related investment has placed greater emphasis on tools and technology than workforce capability development, while only 20% say the greater emphasis has been on developing employees’ skills.
Kaplan argues that the challenge for financial services organisations is therefore not simply to accelerate AI adoption, but to ensure investment in technology is matched by the practical capability needed to use it effectively across the workforce.

Xceptor Expands Investment in Japan to Help Financial Institutions Modernise Capital Markets Operations
summary:
Xceptor, a global leader in data automation for capital markets, today announced it has expanded its investment in Japan to help more financial institutions transform their operating models and drive domestic and international growth.
Xceptor has already established a strong presence in the region, including the launch of its sovereign-grade SaaS offering and strategic partnership with GRCS for local implementation. A Japanese megabank recently selected Xceptor and GRCS to implement Xceptor's SaaS platform, streamlining fragmented post-trade workflows and building a foundation for future innovation.  Xceptor now partners with two of Japan's three megabanks.
As part of its commitment to Japan, Xceptor has appointed Airi Iwamoto as Key Account Director and Satomi Hirono as Principal, Client Success. Both will focus on helping Japanese firms, from large banks to commodities houses (Sogo Shosha), automate mission-critical post-trade processes such as affirmations, confirmations, end-user computing (EUC) remediation, and fund services. Region-specific product capabilities, such as a Japanese-language user interface (UI), are also being rolled out to enable easier adoption and enhance the user experience.
“Many Japanese financial institutions rely on a significant number of disconnected EUC applications and manual processes developed around core banking systems,” said Keith Man, General Manager, APAC at Xceptor. “Any update to a core platform requires extensive testing for each application, adding risk while slowing transformation and AI adoption.”
“Japan’s megabanks are reshaping their Corporate and Investment Banking (CIB) businesses to accelerate global growth,” added Keith Man. “Xceptor already partners with many of the world’s largest banks, and more Japanese firms are looking to draw on our experience to help them on that journey. I’m delighted to welcome Airi and Satomi to the team as we expand our presence in the region.”
Xceptor's Data Automation Platform integrates with clients’ existing internal systems and third-party providers, removing the need for wholesale infrastructure replacement. The platform combines agentic AI with business rules to ingest, validate, and transform data from any system, channel, or format. Multiple validation steps, human-in-the-loop workflows, and full audit trails are embedded for accuracy and control.
